messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid People: avoid other people, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Ellison is a 47-year-old single Black American man who has worked as a city bus driver for nearly fourteen years. He presented for an initial psychological assessment reporting significant distress that has intensified over the past several months, describing sleep difficulties, persistent anger, and a growing sense of isolation from the world around him. His PCL-5 score of 48 places him well within the clinical range for PTSD, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions was one of a man quietly unraveling beneath a surface he has worked hard to keep intact.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Marcus was driving his afternoon route through a commercial district when two police officers boarded his bus in response to a reported disturbance involving another passenger. What followed escalated rapidly. Marcus, who had already begun to de-escalate the situation on his own, was ordered off the bus by the officers and, in the confusion of their commands, was physically restrained against the exterior of the vehicle. He was pushed face-first against the side of the bus, his hands wrenched behind his back, his cheek pressed against the warm metal. He was held there, in full view of his passengers and the street, for what he estimates was several minutes before the officers accepted that he was the driver and not the subject of the call. No apology was offered. He was handed back his keys and told to move the bus along.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus continued working because he needed the income, but something had shifted. Without warning, the image of his own reflection in the bus's side mirror — distorted, pressed flat — would surface in his mind mid-route, arriving with the same physical jolt as the moment itself. Talking about the incident, even in passing, became intolerable; when his dispatcher asked him to file an incident report, Marcus sat with the form for three days before throwing it away. He had come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that nothing would come of telling anyone, that the account would be used against him rather than for him.

His threat monitoring sharpened into something exhausting. At home each night he checked his door locks repeatedly before he could settle — not once, but in circuits, touching each bolt more than he could count. At work, his concentration fractured easily; he missed a stop he had driven for a decade, drawing a complaint that was placed in his file. When a patrol car pulled alongside his bus at a red light, Marcus felt his jaw clench and his knuckles whiten on the wheel. He was certain, in those moments, that the world extended no safety to men like him.

Over the following months, the habits that had felt protective began to cost him in ways he had not anticipated. He stopped attending the Sunday dinners hosted by his church community, a ritual he had kept for years. He avoided the informal conversations with regular passengers that had once been a genuine source of satisfaction in his work. On bad days he would cover his face with his hands in the break room, not wanting anyone to see his expression, and he kept a Bluetooth speaker in his cab, filling the silences with music loud enough to crowd out his own thoughts. He had come to feel that his community — the neighborhood he drove through daily, the congregation he had belonged to for over a decade — was no longer accessible to him, as though the event had placed him on the other side of a window he could see through but not open. People, he had concluded, simply could not be trusted to protect or believe him.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment of rage that frightened him. A passenger questioned his route, and Marcus's response was so sharp, so disproportionate, that he sat in the parking lot afterward shaking, unable to account for himself. He made the appointment the following day. What he said he most feared, sitting in the intake room, was that the person he had been before that afternoon was simply gone. What he hoped, more quietly, was that someone might tell him otherwise.
